strengths: Strong and consistent empirical results across multiple benchmarks, architectures, and scales, with impressive efficiency gains (1.26B matching 2.8B performance with 55% fewer parameters)
Well-executed technical approach using Jacobi iteration for parallelization, with clear mathematical justification and demonstrated rapid convergence
Comprehensive experimental evaluation including large-scale pretraining, extensive downstream tasks, instruction-following benchmarks, and thorough ablation studies
Excellent reproducibility with provided code, detailed hyperparameters, and clear methodology presentation
Validated generalization across Pythia, LLaMA, and GPT-2 architectures, plus successful application to continual pretraining of existing models
weaknesses: Insufficient theoretical justification for why feeding hidden states as embeddings improves performance; lacks mechanistic explanation and analysis of what latent thoughts actually learn

Training-inference mismatch: Jacobi iteration approximates fixed-point hidden states during training but inference uses sequential single-pass generation; approximation quality not verified for downstream tasks
Limited evidence of scalability beyond 1.4B parameters; primary experiments and appendix scale only to 1.4B, with continual pretraining using only 5B tokens on a 3B model

Practical efficiency claims need clarification: Table 3 shows lower throughput (111.55 vs 110.50 tokens/s) than LLaMA-2.8B despite efficiency gains; sequential inference latency not fully captured in FLOP analysis

Moderate novelty: core concept of recurrent hidden-state computation builds incrementally on existing work (Universal Transformers, PonderLM); Jacobi iteration is a known technique applied to this setting
Critical design choice (position embedding reuse) justified only by 'negligible difference' on small models (Pythia-70M with 30B tokens); implications for long-context capabilities unexplored
Missing interpretability analysis: no visualization or probing of latent thought representations; no investigation of which positions benefit most or when latent computation helps/hurts
Baseline comparisons use reported numbers for some methods (PonderLM) rather than reimplementation; some baselines (OPT, Bloom) trained on different data amounts
